Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Their answer was to try to reconcile the different verses.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

They had to interpret the verses that seemed to support predestination in a way that moved beyond their surface meaning, so that they would no longer contradict the other verses they used as evidence for human free will.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Perhaps the earliest roughly systematic example of this approach appears in the letter attributed to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and said to have been written to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān. We discussed earlier al-Shahrastānī’s doubts about whether al-Ḥasan really wrote it. But whether its author was al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, or someone else, the letter is clearly written from a Qadarite point of view. It therefore shows us how the Qadarites tried to reconcile Qurʾanic verses that seemed to contradict one another on predestination and human freedom.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The letter responds to the determinists’ use of the verse:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“God leads astray whomever He wills and guides whomever He wills.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Both actions in this verse—leading astray and guiding—are attributed to God.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

According to the letter, as quoted by Ibn al-Murtaḍā in al-Munya wa-l-Amal (pp. 12–15), those who say that God Himself leads astray whomever He wishes and guides whomever He wishes would understand the matter differently if they looked at the verses before and after this one.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
They would then see that God leads astray only people who were already astray before God “led them astray.” The letter supports this reading with another verse:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

This verse says that God’s act of “leading astray” applies to wrongdoers—people who were already doing wrong beforehand. They had wronged themselves by their own choice when they chose disobedience or unbelief.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This means that when God saw that they had gone astray, He judged them according to the state they had already brought upon themselves.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The letter supports this interpretation with another verse:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“When they went astray, God made their hearts go astray.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The point here is that “God made their hearts go astray” comes after “they went astray.” The second action is presented as the result of the first.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

The phrase “when they went astray” refers to something that had already happened. Their own act of going astray therefore came first in time, while God’s act of making their hearts go astray came afterward.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Their going astray was therefore the cause of God making their hearts go astray.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
From this explanation, we can see that the Qadarites’ method of reconciling Qurʾanic verses on predestination and free will rested on two principles.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
First, God leads astray only those who have already gone astray by themselves and through their own choice.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Second, when the Qurʾan says that God “leads these people astray,” this does not mean that God creates their misguidance in them. Their misguidance already exists through their own will. How could God bring into existence something that already exists? That would be impossible.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Rather, phrases such as “God leads astray” and “God made their hearts go astray” mean that God judges these people to be astray. He declares the reality that already exists, and in doing so establishes the reason why they deserve punishment for what they themselves chose to do.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
We do not have other historical texts showing how the earliest founders of the Qadarite movement applied this method.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
We have found no statement from Maʿbad al-Juhanī explaining how he reconciled Qurʾanic verses that seemed to point in opposite directions on this question.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Nor do we have a clear statement from Ghaylān al-Dimashqī applying this method. What survives of his discussions goes little beyond setting out the general theoretical principles of the Qadarite position.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Two aims stand out in Ghaylān’s arguments.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The first is political. He wants to expose the abuses committed by the rulers of his time—that is, the Umayyads.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The second is theoretical. He wants to defend the justice of religious obligations: God’s right to command people to do certain things and forbid them from doing others.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This defense rests on the principle of justice.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

For Ghaylān, if God is just, He can only command people to do something, or forbid them from doing it, if they genuinely have the power either to act or not to act. In other words, they must be capable of choosing.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Predestination denies them this ability. But if people have no real power either to act or to refrain from acting, then commanding them and punishing them becomes unjust.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Both sides of Ghaylān’s argument—the political and the theoretical—can be seen clearly in his discussion with ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz quoted earlier.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The political side appears when he tells ʿUmar:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“You have begun to see, ʿUmar, though only just. You have begun to look, though only just. Know, ʿUmar, that you have found Islam reduced to a worn-out garment and a fading trace among the dead. You see no path left for us to follow, and hear no voice from which we can benefit. The Sunna has been pushed aside, and religious innovation has spread. The learned man is frightened into silence, while the ignorant man is not even allowed to ask about what he does not know. Sometimes a community may be saved by its leader. So consider which kind of leader you are: the just leader or the unjust one. God does not say, ‘Come to the Fire,’ because then no one would follow Him. Those who call people to the Fire are those who call them to disobey God...”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Here Ghaylān points to the social and religious corruption of his time, and argues that this corruption has grown out of the rulers’ intimidation of the people and their encouragement of wrongdoing.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The second, theoretical part appears in the rest of the discussion, when Ghaylān says:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“Tell me, ʿUmar: have you ever known a wise man to condemn what he himself does...”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
and continues with the passage quoted earlier, whose theoretical meaning we have already explained.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

The only surviving practical example of this method of reconciling conflicting Qurʾanic verses on predestination and free will among the earliest founders of the Qadarite movement is therefore the letter attributed to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

The Muʿtazilites, however, began from the Qadarite position, developed it further, and built its theoretical foundations on philosophical reasoning. In doing so, they made the method much clearer. They applied rational interpretation to Islamic texts from both the Qurʾan and the Sunna.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
We will examine this when we come to the Muʿtazila.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

When we examined the history of the problem of predestination earlier in this chapter, we saw that it had already been raised during the earliest period of Islam, before al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Maʿbad al-Juhanī, and Ghaylān al-Dimashqī.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
From this we concluded that the problem did not arise because of foreign influence. Nor did it arise from some purely philosophical need, detached from the realities of life.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
There is a striking feature of the Qurʾan that deserves some attention here.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Most of the verses that seem to support human freedom of action are Meccan verses, while most of those that seem to support predestination are Medinan.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
De Boer discusses this only indirectly, as part of the wider problem of apparent contradictions in the Qurʾan over “predestination and free choice.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
He explains these differences by pointing to the changing circumstances of the Prophet’s life and to changes in his psychological state.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

We find a similar explanation among some Orientalists, such as H. Grimme in his book on the life and teachings of Muḥammad. Grimme argues that contradictions between Qurʾanic passages came from changes in the Prophet’s psychological state and from the different stages of his mission.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The explanation shared by De Boer and Grimme clearly relies on a psychological method for understanding religious and historical events.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

This is a subjective idealist method. It treats psychological states as the decisive cause behind historical developments. The real conditions of life matter only because of the feelings and personal reactions they produce in an individual. Those feelings then become the main force driving and directing historical events.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Applied to our subject, this means explaining the Islamic movement as a whole, with all its different features, primarily through its connection to the Prophet as an individual and through his personal psychological reactions to the circumstances around him.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
That begins from a very narrow center.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
It does not even fit the Islamic understanding of the Prophet himself, which sees him as the person who delivers a divine message through revelation.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The commentator on De Boer’s book gives another explanation for the emphasis on freedom of choice in the Meccan verses.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

According to him, the general direction of these verses was aimed at “destroying the fatalistic and submissive spirit that had come down to the Arabs from the pre-Islamic period, as shown both by their poetry and by verses of the Qurʾan itself.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This explanation is closer to historical reality and to the actual development of the Islamic movement.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
But the commentator does not explain why the later Medinan verses tend in the opposite, more deterministic direction.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
In our view, the reason is that the Medinan verses came at a time when Islam, after the Hijra and after achieving a degree of stability, faced a new situation.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

It now needed to work out its theoretical and ideological framework in matters of belief and law. It also needed to put that framework into practice, so that the Islamic movement could advance toward its goals and face the future rather than remain tied only to the relationships of the past.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

This helps explain something we already discussed in the first volume of this study: during the period after the Hijra, the Prophet did not welcome arguments over matters of belief. The same was true of the first Rightly Guided Caliphs. They disliked such disputes and called instead for complete religious acceptance of what the Qurʾan taught and what the Prophet decided.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This attitude can be seen clearly in the following Qurʾanic instruction:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“If they argue with you, say: I have submitted myself to God, and so have those who follow me...”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

This Medinan verse instructed Muslims to answer people who argued with them over matters of belief by saying, in effect: We have submitted ourselves to God, and there is no room for argument about that.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This was the situation during the Prophet’s lifetime and during the first period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
But the social and political conflicts that emerged toward the end of the Rightly Guided period, and then became much more intense under the Umayyad state, created a completely different situation.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Under these new conditions, the door to debate could no longer remain closed, even in matters of belief.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The problem of predestination was one of the first issues to become the subject of unavoidable debate.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

The reason was that social and political developments had drawn increasingly clear lines between the ruling class and those who benefited from it, on one side, and the groups suffering different forms of injustice under those rulers, on the other.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The ruling class then began to use the idea of predestination for its own purposes. It turned the doctrine into a religious argument for preserving its rule and keeping its authority over the people.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

It was natural, under these conditions, for the idea of predestination to become deeply rooted in the minds of most ordinary believers throughout the Umayyad period. They repeatedly heard Qurʾanic passages whose surface meaning seemed to support it.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
They must also have heard preachers and mosque speakers explain these verses in ways that reinforced this deterministic reading.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Over time, many came to believe that everything they suffered—the hardships of life and the injustice of rulers alike—had been fixed for them by fate and divine decree. They were left with no choice but to submit to suffering and oppression because these had supposedly been eternally decreed by God.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This is where the idea of predestination began to take its place in the history of Arab-Islamic thought.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
It was also here that it began to acquire an ideological dimension, expressing the class outlook of the political institution—that is, the state.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Of course, some people do not see, or do not want to see, any direct connection between the idea of predestination as a religious or intellectual doctrine and this ideological role.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
It may indeed be true that no direct connection existed.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
But that does not mean there was no indirect connection.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Speaking about the state after it had become a power standing independently over society, Engels writes that once this happened, it “created a new ideological revolution.” He explains that among professional politicians and theorists of state and civil law, the connection with economic realities can disappear almost completely from view.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Engels then says that higher forms of ideology—that is, forms further removed from their material and economic base—take the shape of philosophy and religion. The link between ideas and the material conditions in which people live becomes less and less direct and increasingly hidden behind a chain of intermediate connections.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Basra was the first setting from which the Qadarite movement emerged.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

As we saw earlier, it first appeared in the school of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī. Maʿbad al-Juhanī then entered the movement and became an active advocate for it, not only in Basra but also in the Ḥijāz. His influence later reached Syria through Ghaylān al-Dimashqī.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Why did this happen in Basra?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The answer lies in two features that marked the city throughout the Umayyad period in particular.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The first was that Basra had become a gathering place for many different political forces, parties, and intellectual movements opposed to Umayyad rule.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
These included the Shīʿa, the Khārijites, and the mawālī, many of whom came from different earlier religious traditions.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Basra was also a major center for large groups of craftsmen, agricultural workers, slaves, and poor small traders who had arrived from many different regions in search of work or while fleeing persecution by landowners.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The second feature followed largely from the first.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Basra was one of the places where Umayyad oppression appeared most openly.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
On one side, this oppression was directed against political parties and intellectual movements that opposed Umayyad rule for one reason or another.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
On the other, it fell on the weaker groups in society: craftsmen, agricultural workers, slaves, poor small traders, and people with almost nothing.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Their lives were marked by severe exploitation, forced labor, oppression, misery, and poverty.
